title: Cursor-bound complete backup generation
description: Objective: implement the production BackupGeneration capability required before CORE-S14 can restore anything. Deliverable: a @moe/store backup-generation module that snapshots the project SQLite database at one committed global cursor and builds/verifies a canonical signed manifest over the database plus every caller-declared reachable artifact, receipt, context, manifest, and public-key-chain object (digest and byte length). MEASURED GAP at HEAD 1ce0059: @moe/store has WAL/full-sync durability and cursor reads, while @moe/runner has artifact verification, but `rg` finds no BackupGeneration type, backup API, generation manifest, or verifier anywhere in packages/*/src or apps/*/src. NOT in scope: two-slot installation, recovery-incarnation minting, external-effect inventory, R3 completion, fault fixtures, release publication, or editing the authoritative design. Hard dependencies: existing @moe/store and @moe/runner artifact contracts only. Owned paths: packages/store/src/backup-generation.* and focused package export wiring only. Verification: pnpm --filter @moe/store typecheck && pnpm --filter @moe/store test.
definitionOfDone: The production API snapshots SQLite at one explicit committed cursor N and returns a frozen versioned manifest binding project identity, cursor/RPO, database digest/size, complete declared object closure, verification-key chain, and source-generation digest.

A generation is marked complete only after every listed byte source re-verifies by digest and size; any missing, unreadable, extra, duplicate, mixed-generation, or unverifiable object returns stable `BACKUP_PROOF_UNKNOWN` at layer `BACKUP_GENERATION`, truth `UNKNOWN`, and no restorable manifest.
Manifest canonicalization, digest, and signature verification are deterministic and reject cursor/database/object/key-chain tampering with stable reason codes asserted against the production surface.

Focused tests exercise a real temporary SQLite file plus real object bytes, assert at least one object in every configured closure category, and mutation-check one production verifier branch so a zero-case or helper-only proof cannot pass.

1. THE SEATED-SNAPSHOT BACKUP WORKS AS THE PLAN DESCRIBES. Built a real WAL database, seated a read snapshot on a dedicated `new DatabaseSync(path, { readOnly: true })` with `PRAGMA query_only=ON` + `BEGIN DEFERRED` + a tail read (seated tail = 3), then committed a further row on the live writer (live tail = 4) BEFORE awaiting the backup. Result: `backup()` returned 3 pages and the produced image reads MAX(global_position) = 3, not 4. So the post-seat commit is genuinely outside the captured generation, which is exactly the RPO property DoD 1 requires. The backup image comes out in `journal_mode=wal`.
   API CORRECTION worth recording: `backup` is a STANDALONE async export of node:sqlite — `const { DatabaseSync, backup } = require("node:sqlite")` — and `DatabaseSync.prototype.backup` is `undefined`. Anyone reading "node:sqlite.backup" as a method will write code that does not exist. node:sqlite exports exactly: DatabaseSync, Session, StatementSync, backup, constants.

ED25519 IS AVAILABLE AND BEHAVES. `crypto.generateKeyPairSync("ed25519")`, `crypto.sign(null, msg, privateKey)` -> 64-byte signature, verify true on the signed bytes and FALSE on tampered bytes. `publicKey.export({ type: "spki", format: "der" })` -> 44 bytes, which is the stable form to carry in the key chain. Signing takes `null` as the algorithm argument for Ed25519; passing a hash name throws.

implementationPlan.description: Implement the pure manifest/trust boundary. Define immutable exact-key request/manifest/container/result types and closed reason vocabulary; defensively snapshot hostile inputs in one synchronous pass before any async work; normalize well-formed NFC identifiers and `/` logical paths; represent cursor and byte sizes as canonical nonnegative decimal strings; reject unknown fields, accessors/proxies, sparse arrays, duplicate normalized identities/destinations, mixed source-generation digests, and incomplete category sets. Produce one deterministic sorted-key canonical byte projection that excludes only its self-digest, compute the SHA-256 generation digest, sign the complete digest-bearing manifest with signature structurally outside it, deep-freeze outputs, and implement the production verifier to recompute digest/inventory and validate the bound leaf/key-rotation chain against caller-supplied external trust before Ed25519 verification. Map every parse/digest/trust/crypto false-or-throw condition to the exact non-authoritative failure tuple without leaking a restorable manifest.

VERIFIER ORDER IS DELIBERATE AND FAILS CLOSED AT EACH STAGE: container shape -> closure structure -> recomputed generation digest -> observed inventory -> external key anchoring -> Ed25519 signature. Anchoring precedes verification specifically so a replacement key travelling inside the container can never self-authorize, and the signature is checked against the ANCHORED key bytes rather than the carried ones. That is the difference between a proof and a self-signed assertion, and it is why `MANIFEST_SIGNATURE_INVALID` (not a trust code) is the correct answer when the anchor names the right keyId but different bytes.

SECOND DEVIATION, and it makes the module honest rather than convenient: `verifyBackupGeneration` takes an optional `observedLogicalPaths`. The plan has the verifier "recompute digest/inventory", but a directory listing is an I/O observation and this module must stay pure to be testable without a filesystem. So the inventory is CALLER-SUPPLIED — the step-4 coordinator passes a real listing, and the port pattern matches how the rest of this repo handles observations. Consequence worth stating plainly: omitting the option means "inventory not observed", which is NOT the same as "inventory verified", and the coordinator must always supply it. The step-2 test was updated to match, and it now also asserts the same container VERIFIES with a truthful listing — so the INVENTORY_MISMATCH refusal is attributable to the inventory and not to some unrelated field.

DEFENSIVE DETAILS THAT ARE EASY TO GET SILENTLY WRONG, each written for a specific attack:
- Sparse arrays: `Array.prototype.every` SKIPS holes, so a sparse descriptor array would pass an `every`-based shape check while carrying undefined entries. `Object.keys(objects).length !== objects.length` rejects it before the element check runs.
- Case-folded destination collision: duplicate detection folds `logicalPath` to lowercase, because a case-insensitive filesystem would otherwise collapse two "distinct" destinations into one file AFTER the check passed.
- Backslash in logical paths is rejected outright. On Windows it is a separator the `/`-segment traversal check would not otherwise see, so `..\\escape` would slip through a POSIX-only reading.
- Canonical bytes exclude ONLY `generationDigest`, the field they produce. Keys are emitted sorted at every level and both `objects` and `keyChain` are sorted by id, so caller ordering cannot change the digest — which is what makes the step-2 permuted-order determinism test meaningful.
- Cursor and byte lengths are canonical decimal STRINGS validated by regex. `global_position` is a bigint column; a JS number loses precision past 2^53 and would corrupt the single value the whole generation is bound to.
- Crypto failures are caught and mapped to the frozen tuple. A malformed key and a forged signature are indistinguishable here and both are non-authoritative, so neither throws out of the verifier.

implementationPlan.description: Implement the Node/SQLite generation coordinator behind store-owned filesystem, hashing, signing, and verification ports (no @moe/runner import). From the existing store health/path seam, open a dedicated read-only DatabaseSync, set query_only, `BEGIN DEFERRED`, validate schema/application id/project binding, seat the WAL snapshot by reading the exact tail `global_position`, refuse a cursor mismatch before publishing, and await `node:sqlite.backup` while the transaction stays open. Reopen the staged image read-only, run quick/integrity and foreign-key checks, prove the same project and exact cursor, then close and stream-hash its bytes. In an exclusive staging directory under the final parent, copy each snapshotted declared object through descriptor write loops while hashing/size-checking, fsync and reread every file, write/sign/verify the canonical manifest only after all payload bytes pass, close handles, atomically rename the whole directory, persist the rename cross-platform (POSIX parent-directory fsync; Windows reopen/fsync the final manifest), enumerate and reverify the exact final set through the production verifier, and only then return authority. Refuse unsafe aliases or non-identical existing targets, and on any SQLite/fs/crypto/cleanup uncertainty close resources, best-effort remove staging, leave no partial final manifest, and return the stable UNKNOWN tuple.

THE ORDERING IS THE GUARANTEE. Nothing reaches the final path until every declared byte is copied, re-read and verified AND the container has passed the same production verifier a consumer would run. Sequence: seal request synchronously -> closure inspection -> destination safety -> staging root -> capture at cursor -> copy/verify each object -> build manifest -> sign -> self-verify through `verifyBackupGeneration` -> persist manifest -> atomic directory rename -> reopen and fsync the published manifest -> re-read from disk and verify AGAIN -> only then return authority.

TWO VERIFICATIONS, DELIBERATELY NOT ONE. The in-memory container is checked before publishing, and the bytes actually on disk are re-read and checked after the rename. A single in-memory check would prove the object I just built is consistent with itself, not that what landed is restorable — and the rename is exactly where a partial write would show up.

DETAILS CHOSEN AGAINST SPECIFIC FAILURES:
- The cursor comparison happens BEFORE any bytes are published, so a mismatched request never leaves a partial generation behind.
- `BEGIN DEFERRED` acquires nothing until its first read, so the tail read is what actually pins the snapshot. The comment says so, because "begin then backup" without the read looks equivalent and is not.
- The staged image is validated in its own right — quick_check, foreign_key_check, project binding, and the exact cursor — rather than trusting that a successful copy implies a sound database.
- `application_id` is checked against the store's own `SQLITE_APPLICATION_ID` before anything else, so a foreign SQLite file cannot be captured as if it were a project database.
- The public key is DERIVED from the private key with `createPublicKey`, never accepted from the caller, so a container cannot advertise a key its signature was not made with.
- Database digest is streamed via `createReadStream`, not buffered: a project database can be multiple GiB and `readFile` would trade a correctness win for an OOM.
- Cursor is read as `CAST(... AS TEXT)` in SQL. Reading a bigint column into a JS number loses precision past 2^53 and would corrupt the single value the generation is bound to.
- The staging root is removed in a `finally`, and the rollback of a seated read transaction is attempted before the handle closes — Windows holds locks that make a leaked handle a later EBUSY rather than an obvious failure.

ONE TEST DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED, AND IT WAS MINE, NOT THE PRODUCTION CODE'S. The determinism test originally built two SEPARATE harnesses and compared their `generationDigest`. It failed with MIXED_SOURCE_GENERATION — a correct production refusal, because the second harness's descriptors carried their own generation digest while the request overrode it. Fixing only that would still have left the test unsound: two harnesses have two different databases, so `databaseDigest` differs and the comparison would have proved nothing about canonicalization even when green. Rewritten to build ONE database and object set twice into distinct destination roots with permuted descriptor order, which is the property actually claimed. Worth flagging to QA as the interesting one: the first version would have passed with a lucky implementation and proved nothing.

A REAL PRODUCTION DEFECT WAS FOUND HERE, BY A TEST THAT LOOKED LIKE A NITPICK. Asserting "no `database.sqlite-wal` in the published generation" failed — and it was not a test artifact. `validateStagedImage` opens the staged image read-only to run quick_check/foreign_key_check, and opening a WAL database leaves `-wal` and `-shm` sidecars beside it. Those were being renamed into the final generation.

Why that matters rather than being untidy: the manifest's `databaseDigest` covers `database.sqlite` ALONE. A sidecar riding along is content that changes what restores while breaking no digest and failing no signature — undeclared bytes inside a signed generation. The inventory check could not catch it either, because the coordinator passes only the manifest's declared logical paths as the observed set.

Fixed in production, not in the test: sidecars are removed after validation and BEFORE hashing, so `databaseDigest` covers the final bytes. The comment in `backup-generation-capture.ts` states the reason, because "delete the -wal" reads like cleanup and is actually a correctness fix.

Ordering subtlety worth flagging to QA: the assertion has to run BEFORE the test opens the captured database, since opening it creates a `-wal` of its own. My first version checked after opening and would have been vacuous. That is the same shape as the fixture-derived-from-the-subject trap — the check was measuring its own side effect.

INTEGRATION CASES ADDED:
- Cursor 0 on an empty database. `global_position` CHECKs > 0, so cursor 0 is representable only as "no events captured" — the empty-generation case, not a row at position 0.
- Cursor N with the committed tail proven inside the produced IMAGE, not just claimed in the manifest: the captured `domain_events` has tail "2" and exactly 2 rows, while the live database is separately asserted to have advanced to "3". A manifest can claim cursor 2 over an image holding 3 rows, and that gap is precisely what makes a backup unrestorable at its stated RPO — so the assertion is against the database file.
- Exact per-category counts, not "at least one". Every category present exactly once and `objects.length === 5`: a non-zero check alone would pass an implementation that duplicated a descriptor. Each declared object is then re-hashed off disk and compared to its manifest digest.
- Determinism now also asserts SIGNATURE equality, not only `generationDigest`. Ed25519 is deterministic, so identical canonical bytes must produce an identical signature; comparing only the digest would miss a signer that had drifted onto a different byte projection.

ONE EARLIER TEST WAS UNSOUND AND IS NOW CORRECT, worth stating because it would have passed by luck. The determinism case originally used two separate harnesses. Two harnesses mean two different databases, so `databaseDigest` differs and the comparison proves nothing about canonicalization even when green. Rebuilt to use ONE database and object set, built twice into distinct destination roots with permuted descriptor order — which is the property actually claimed.

REAL ADAPTER ON EVERY RESTORABLE PATH, per the plan: every success case runs the genuine Node/SQLite adapter over a real temp database, real object files and real Ed25519 keys. No injected port fakes a success. The only platform concession remains the `chmod 0o000` unreadable case, which Windows ignores; it asserts the invariant that holds on both platforms — if it refuses, it refuses with OBJECT_UNREADABLE and the full tuple; a restorable claim over unverified bytes is forbidden everywhere.

THE SURVIVOR WAS A REAL COVERAGE GAP, NOT A DRILL ARTIFACT. `observed.length !== declared.size` is redundant with the membership loop beneath it FOR THE CASE I HAD WRITTEN: my inventory test supplied an EXTRA path, which the loop catches on its own. The cardinality comparison exists for the opposite direction — an object MISSING from the final listing — and nothing exercised it. So a published generation that had silently lost a declared object would have verified clean if that line were ever removed, and my suite would not have noticed.

Fixed by adding the missing-object case (`observedLogicalPaths: declared.slice(1)`) rather than by deleting the "redundant" line. Re-drilled: the same mutation now goes RED (1 failed). Restore verified byte-exact against the pre-drill hash `bbe0cbdc2f829f9beff98d7b903482a04a286ca1`, and the suite returned to 26/26 after every restore.

ADVERSARIAL REVIEW — what was attacked and what holds:
- TOCTOU across awaits: caller values are copied out in one synchronous pass in `sealBackupRequest` and never re-read, so a getter or concurrent mutation cannot change what was validated.
- Sparse arrays: `every` skips holes, so own-index count is compared against length before element checks. Covered by a table row.
- Case-fold duplicates: destinations are folded to lowercase, so a case-insensitive filesystem cannot collapse two "distinct" paths into one file after the check passed.
- Source/final aliasing: resolved absolute paths with a trailing separator, so `/data/dbx` is not read as a child of `/data/db`.
- Unbounded buffering: the database is stream-hashed; a multi-GiB image is not read whole.
- Signature self-reference: the signature sits structurally outside the manifest, and canonical bytes exclude only `generationDigest`, the field they produce.
- External key anchoring: verification uses the ANCHORED key bytes, never the carried ones — a container that swapped in its own key fails.
- Authority leakage on exceptions: every catch returns the frozen refusal tuple; the success value and both manifest/container objects are frozen.
- Handle cleanup: staging is removed in `finally`, a seated read transaction is rolled back before its handle closes, and the published manifest is reopened and fsynced because a directory rename is not itself durable on Windows.

ONE ATTACK FOUND A GENUINE PRODUCTION DEFECT EARLIER (step 5) AND IT STAYS FIXED: WAL sidecars left by the validation open were being published beside the image, uncovered by `databaseDigest` — undeclared bytes inside a signed generation. Removed before hashing.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered: Chose a standalone @moe/store createBackupGeneration API over the existing SqliteEventStore health/database-path seam plus a dedicated read-only node:sqlite connection. Rejected copying the live .db/-wal/-shm files because committed WAL pages can be omitted; rejected widening SqliteEventStore or using its synchronous readSnapshotOperation because node:sqlite backup is asynchronous and would outlive that transaction; rejected importing @moe/runner artifact helpers or distribution internals because dependency direction and the task rail forbid it. Use BEGIN DEFERRED, seat the read snapshot by reading the exact tail cursor, await node:sqlite backup on that same read-only connection, and validate the staged image. Use a same-parent staged generation directory, store-owned streaming/fsync/rename/persist/read-back operations, manifest-last staging, atomic directory rename, and final production re-verification. Treat the caller-supplied, defensively snapshotted descriptor set as the sealed complete closure; do not claim repository-wide reachability discovery because no store closure catalog exists. Keep Ed25519 signature outside the canonical digest-bearing manifest and require an external trusted key/chain anchor rather than trusting only carried key bytes.
planningNotes.codebaseInsights: SqliteEventStore.getHealth() exposes the canonical databasePath/project/durability facts without exposing its private core. The event cursor is domain_events.global_position and must be serialized canonically as decimal bigint text. The store is WAL/FULL and current pinned Node 24 node:sqlite backup can preserve an established read transaction while concurrent writers advance the live WAL. Store hostile-input precedents are store-input-primitives.ts, store-input-containers.ts, subscriptions/subscription-doc-codec.ts, and outbox-relay-digests.ts; snapshot every caller object/array/byte field once before the first await, reject accessors/proxies/sparse arrays/unknown keys/-0/ill-formed or non-NFC text, and never reread caller-owned values. Runtime modules use committed one-line .js bridges, and store-runtime-entrypoint.test.ts exercises raw Node loadability. The durable publisher pattern to reproduce (not import) is descriptor write-loop -> fsync -> close -> rename -> persist -> reread/verify, with POSIX parent-directory fsync and Windows final-file reopen/fsync semantics. Downstream consumers already recorded are two-slot anchor task-b6e3dd2af916490fb2bc4d375a530683 and R3 completion task-6f786c58cabf4f85be8ed4135e68a752; exports are not claimed as composition.
planningNotes.risks: Never hash a raw open SQLite main file, buffer multi-GiB payloads, include absolute/temp/platform paths, mtimes, randomness, or clocks in signed bytes, or allow a carried replacement key to self-authorize. Define and test duplicate logical identities/destination paths, mixed source-generation digests, exact bidirectional file inventory, pre-existing final targets, path aliasing, cursor ahead/behind, post-seat concurrent commits, malformed/corrupt SQLite, short reads/writes, crypto false/throw, and every fsync/rename/persist/read-back failure. On all uncertainty return only frozen {ok:false, code:'BACKUP_PROOF_UNKNOWN', layer:'BACKUP_GENERATION', truth:'UNKNOWN', restorable:false, reason:<closed reason>} with no manifest/path/capability; close handles before best-effort cleanup for Windows locking. Verify staged and final bytes through the production verifier and either reverify an identical pre-existing generation or refuse—never rely on overwrite behavior. Keep each production TypeScript source targeted at <=250 physical lines and split before 400; preserve foreign shared-tree work and stage only the six named owned paths.
